1020.bp: When you show someone a video or a stream of events, what grabs their attention? Usually the exciting moments at the start and end. But when a recommendation system watches your viewing history to guess what you'll like next, it needs to pay equal attention to the middle parts—the quiet but informative behaviors—not just fixate on your first and last clicks. The system's architecture is literally broken in a predictable way, and this paper fixes it.
1020.wh: Attention-based systems (the kind that look at a sequence of items and try to understand patterns) have an unexpected quirk: they tend to ignore the middle of the sequence, treating the beginning and end as more important. This happens even when you shuffle the data around, so it is not about where things sit in the sequence—it is baked into how the system is designed. The problem is deep, not superficial.
1020.wp: The authors designed a two-part fix: during training, they selectively mask certain positions to stop the system from over-relying on boundaries; during prediction time, they calibrate the scores the model produces to remove any remaining position-only effects that have nothing to do with actual user interests. It is like teaching a student to stop reading only chapter beginnings, then checking their test answers afterward to catch any remaining bias.
1020.ww: By directly counteracting the architectural quirk during training and then cleaning up the leftover bias at prediction time, the system learns to distribute its attention more fairly across all moments in a user's history. The middle behaviors—which often contain the most meaningful signals about preference—get proper weight again.
1020.po: The fix leads to measurably better ranking quality across multiple datasets. The improvements are consistent because both the training masking and the inference calibration work together: one prevents the model from learning bad habits, the other catches any slips that still occur.

1021.bp: Finding a specific person from a text description in a crowded photo—say, 'tall man with glasses'—is crucial for public safety and criminal investigations. Existing systems fine-tune enormous vision-language models like CLIP on this task, but doing so fully is expensive and the model tends to overfit to narrow examples and fails on new scenarios. There is a smarter way to adapt these massive pre-trained models without retraining the whole thing.
1021.wh: Fine-tuning giant models costs huge amounts of compute and memory. Partially adapting them (using lightweight parameter-efficient methods) keeps costs down, but these methods struggle with the fine details of identity clues and are easily thrown off by noisy training data with mismatched image-text pairs. The system is caught between efficiency and accuracy.
1021.ap: This paper builds a lightweight adapter that captures both broad patterns (the full person silhouette) and fine details (specific facial features) separately, using a multi-level relational approach. It also learns to downweight confusing or wrong training examples on the fly, and adds a cross-modal verification step that checks the image-to-text and text-to-image alignment to catch ambiguous cases where the same text might match multiple people.
1021.ww: By modeling features at multiple scales (coarse and fine), the system picks up both the obvious and subtle identity markers that full fine-tuning would capture, but using far fewer parameters. Downweighting noisy examples prevents the model from learning wrong associations, and the verification step removes ambiguities that would otherwise poison the final ranking.
1021.po: The result is a system that works well on new, unseen people and domains without full retraining. It keeps computational costs low while improving matching accuracy, making it practical for real-world deployment on criminal investigation databases.

1022.bp: A recommendation system that shows you what movies to watch, what songs to listen to, or what products to buy must juggle a tension: people actually enjoy both mainstream hits (the popular things everyone watches) and niche favorites (the obscure gems only they care about). Most systems squash this diversity by letting popular content dominate the signal, drowning out the personalized stuff. The goal is to recommend both fairly.
1022.wh: When a system builds a recommendation model using graph-based learning (a method that treats users and items as nodes in a network and spreads information through connections), it treats all interests the same way. Information from popular items overwhelms the signal, and niche interests get buried. The system has no way to say 'this user cares deeply about indie horror films, even though most people watch blockbusters.'
1022.ap: This paper separates the user-item network into two independent parts: one that models popular interests and one that models niche interests. It does this by decomposing the network signals using frequency-domain math (thinking of interests like sound waves—high frequency for niche, low frequency for popular). It also uses a four-quadrant graph structure that lets the system think about behaviors and popularity separately, then combines them through multiple supervised learning tasks at once.
1022.ww: By splitting the network into two pathways, each interest type is modeled with its own logic and weight. Popular interests do not drown out niche ones because they are on separate channels. The frequency decomposition is based on a real principle: similar frequencies should influence similar things, so popular and niche interests, which have different 'frequencies', naturally separate.
1022.po: Across four real production datasets, the system recommends items with both higher accuracy (people like more of what it suggests) and better diversity (it actually surfaces niche items alongside mainstream ones). Users get better personalization because the system respects both the hits they watch and the deep cuts they treasure.

1023.bp: When you ask a question like 'which countries have a population over 100 million?', the answer might live in a table buried in some Wikipedia article. Yet finding that table is hard because the structure of the table (rows and columns) does not immediately tell you what it contains semantically. Most systems need labeled examples to learn the connection between queries and tables, making them useless when no training data exists. This paper finds tables with zero labeled examples.
1023.wh: Existing table retrieval systems either mangle the table into text (losing structure) or require large labeled datasets showing which tables answer which questions. In a cold-start scenario—day one with a new table corpus and no queries yet—both approaches fail. The system must infer meaning from the table's own structure and content without any external guidance.
1023.ap: Instead of learning from query-table pairs, this system learns the structure of the entire table corpus first. It represents each table using both its internal structure (columns, data types) and links to external knowledge graphs (like Wikidata). At search time, it uses three retrieval signals in parallel: dense semantic matching (like traditional search), symbolic graph traversal (following connections in the knowledge graph), and sparse keyword matching (exact term matches). These three signals are combined dynamically based on the query.
1023.ww: By modeling the corpus itself rather than query-table pairs, the system grounds its understanding in what the tables actually contain. The external knowledge graph links provide semantic anchors (e.g., 'population' is a demographic attribute). The hybrid retrieval approach—combining dense, symbolic, and sparse methods—means no single weakness matters: if keywords work, great; if the structure is clear, that works too; if semantic similarity helps, it will be found.
1023.po: On public benchmarks, the system retrieves the right tables with high precision and recall, even for implicit queries where the connection between question and table is not obvious. It works on day one with no labeled training data, solving the cold-start problem that plagues existing methods.

1024.bp: A legal researcher trying to find relevant court cases from thousands of documents needs precision—every wrong result wastes time and can lead to bad arguments. The standard approach runs a fast, coarse search first, then a slower, detailed re-ranking step second. But when the fast search misses the target, the slow step cannot fix it, and when the fast and slow steps disagree, quality suffers. A unified system could do both jobs better.
1024.wh: Two-stage retrieval pipelines suffer from cascade errors: if the first stage filters out the right document, the second stage will never see it. Also, the fast and slow stages may have learned contradictory signals, so they pull in different directions. And both stages can assign high confidence to documents that are actually irrelevant—a 'phantom hit' that breaks the ranking.
1024.ap: This paper builds a single model that does both retrieval and re-ranking at once, with shared weights between them. To stop the phantom-hit problem, it trains the model to see pure-negative document groups (documents that are definitely wrong), teaches it to be uncertain about borderline cases, and uses entropy regularization to avoid overconfident wrong answers. The training objective pushes different margins of confidence for different difficulty levels.
1024.ww: By unifying the stages, errors do not cascade: the model reasons about the full document space at once. By explicitly training on pure-negatives and penalizing overconfidence, the model learns to say 'I do not know' rather than guess. The entropy regularization means the model spreads its confidence more fairly, so truly relevant documents stand out.
1024.po: On legal benchmarks, the system beats both independent two-stage pipelines and other unified approaches, achieving state-of-the-art precision and recall for legal document retrieval. The improvement is especially large on borderline cases where confidence calibration matters most.

1025.bp: Recommendation systems running on phones and smart watches need to use very little memory and power. Yet most systems store recommendation models with high-precision numbers that take up megabytes. Quantization shrinks the model by using low-precision numbers, but doing so naively (rounding all numbers the same way) loses accuracy. For recommendation systems with complex network structures, a smarter quantization strategy can keep accuracy high.
1025.wh: Graph-based recommendation models treat users and items as nodes in a network. The numbers attached to each node (called embeddings) vary wildly—some nodes are similar to many others, while some are unique. Quantizing all embeddings with the same precision scheme does not work because a uniform quantization breaks the delicate differences between nodes. The system needs to understand which nodes are easily confused and which need more precision.
1025.ap: Instead of quantizing all dimensions of an embedding uniformly, this paper groups the dimensions of each node's embedding into multiple chunks based on how their values spread. Then it quantizes each chunk separately. During training with the model still learning, the chunk boundaries are learned dynamically. After training, the system clusters similar nodes and applies chunk-wise quantization based on what it learned. Some nodes get fine-grained chunks (more precision), others get coarse chunks (faster, smaller).
1025.ww: By treating each chunk independently, the quantization respects the actual distribution of values in the network. Nodes that are similar get similar quantization, preserving the neighborhood structure that the recommendation algorithm relies on. The dynamic learning during training means the model learns what precision is actually needed for each part of each node.
1025.po: Across multiple real datasets, the quantized models match the accuracy of full-precision models while using far less memory and compute. This makes it practical to run recommendation systems directly on resource-limited devices without losing recommendation quality.

1026.bp: Given a single 2D photograph of a scene, find all the 3D models in a library that match it. This is hard because a 2D image and a 3D model are fundamentally different: they express the world in different dimensions and from different viewpoints. Most prior work needs labeled 3D-to-2D pairs to learn the bridge, but labeling is expensive. This paper learns the bridge with no such labels.
1026.wh: The 2D-to-3D gap is enormous: a 2D image loses depth, a 3D model has no single viewpoint, and categories have imbalanced representation (some objects are common, others rare). Previous unsupervised methods get confused by these gaps, and their decision boundaries for 'same object' versus 'different object' drift differently in the 2D and 3D spaces. Also, not all neighbors of a query image should be equally important; some are more structurally similar than others.
1026.ap: This paper attacks the problem in three coordinated ways. First, it carefully constructs mini-batches that balance category representation so rare objects are not ignored. Second, it uses an adversarial technique to align the decision boundaries between the 2D and 3D worlds—making the model prefer sharp separation between similar and dissimilar objects in both spaces equally. Third, it builds a cross-modal graph showing which 2D and 3D samples are neighbors, then spreads this relational structure through the model, ensuring that the neighborhood relationships discovered in one modality are preserved in the other.
1026.ww: The balanced batches prevent category bias. The aligned decision boundaries mean 'close' and 'far apart' have the same meaning in both modality spaces. The graph-based neighborhood consistency is a direct signal: if two images are neighbors in the 2D space, their matched 3D models should be neighbors too. This preserves the semantic structure that the model learns.
1026.po: On benchmark datasets for image-based 3D model retrieval, the system consistently outperforms prior unsupervised methods, finding the matching 3D models with higher accuracy. The improvements come entirely from smarter use of unlabeled data, no additional labels needed.

1027.bp: Depression is a silent disease—people often hide symptoms in public. But social media reveals spontaneous, unfiltered behavior: the videos someone posts, the tone of their voice, the visual style they choose. Mining these signals from real social media data could enable early screening at scale, far earlier than clinical detection. The challenge is combining visual (video) and acoustic (audio tone) information intelligently.
1027.wh: Combining multiple types of data (modalities) is hard because they speak different languages: a video frame shows what someone looks like, but audio tone shows how they feel, and these do not directly relate. Naive fusion methods just average or concatenate the signals, missing the fact that visual and audio should inform each other. Also, there is a gap in what each modality means—visual and acoustic features are fundamentally different and hard to align.
1027.ap: This paper builds a system where visual and audio information guide each other dynamically. It constructs a graph showing which visual samples are similar to which audio samples, finding complementary information (visual cues the audio misses, and vice versa). For each modality separately, it uses a graph-informed residual learning approach (adding small learned corrections to base features, guided by the graph structure). After refining each modality separately, it fuses them together and makes a final prediction.
1027.ww: By having modalities guide each other, the system learns which visual signals matter for depression and which audio signals matter, rather than treating them as separate problems. The graph explicitly captures cross-modal relationships, so the refining step for audio is informed by what visual cues mean. The residual approach adds only small, targeted corrections, preserving each modality's integrity while improving alignment.
1027.po: Tested on real social media depression datasets, the system detects depression more accurately than methods that ignore the cross-modal guidance. The improvements are consistent, suggesting the mutual guidance actually captures meaningful patterns in how depression manifests across visual and acoustic behavior.

1028.bp: When recommending a sequence of items (like a playlist or a binge-watch order), systems often think in frequency-domain terms, decomposing a user's preference patterns into high-frequency (recent, quick changes) and low-frequency (stable, long-term) signals. Yet most systems handle both simultaneously in one model, not recognizing that short-term mood shifts and long-term taste require different reasoning. A smarter system treats them separately.
1028.wh: Frequency-domain reasoning in recommendations is powerful but crude: amplifying high-frequency signals to capture recent trends also amplifies random noise. Also, short-term and long-term preferences have different temporal rhythms and should use different model paths. One model trying to do both ends up compromising on both. The system needs dedicated pathways for different timescales.
1028.ap: This paper separates the recommendation model into distinct pathways: one for long-term preference (stable, low-frequency patterns) and one for short-term preference (recent, high-frequency shifts). For noise handling, it intelligently suppresses low-energy noise in each frequency band while keeping the important signal components. The two pathways make their predictions independently, then a learned gate dynamically decides how much weight to give each pathway based on the current context.
1028.ww: By decomposing into separate pathways, each pathway can be tuned for its own temporal characteristics. The energy-aware denoising respects the fact that some frequency bands are inherently noisier than others—it adapts to each band's energy distribution rather than using a one-size-fits-all denoising. The dynamic gate means long-term taste dominates when the user is browsing calmly, but short-term mood matters when they are actively searching.
1028.po: On five real datasets, the system improves ranking metrics (how well predicted rankings match user clicks) by average of 6.67%, with particularly large gains in capturing recent preference shifts. The noise suppression also improves stability, reducing spiky incorrect predictions.

1029.bp: Large multimodal models (systems that see both images and text) can make mistakes—maybe they misidentify a person or get a fact wrong. Retraining the entire model is impractical. In-context editing offers a shortcut: can you fix a specific mistake just by adding context to the input, without changing the model weights? The challenge is controlling which part of the model actually makes the edit.
1029.wh: Naive in-context editing (just adding corrective context to the input) is unreliable because the model might ignore the context or misunderstand which mistake to fix. The system needs to know precisely which neurons or components inside the model are responsible for the error and which context matters. Without this targeting, editing feels like a lucky guess.
1029.ap: This paper identifies specific neurons inside the model that are involved in the mistake (called 'contextual neurons'). It then selectively updates only those neurons with context-aware changes. The identification process looks at which neurons respond to both the image and the text context. The editing step then injects new information into exactly those identified neurons, leaving the rest of the model untouched.
1029.ww: By targeting specific neurons, the edit affects only the relevant reasoning path inside the model. The system does not need to retrain anything; it just modulates internal signals at inference time. This is like knowing exactly which neuron in a brain cares about 'who is in this photo' and nudging just that one, rather than dosing the whole brain with a medicine.
1029.po: Tested on three popular large multimodal models with benchmark edits (correcting wrong associations between images and descriptions), the system successfully fixes mistakes without affecting unrelated knowledge. The neuron-level approach is more targeted and reliable than previous in-context editing methods that just add context blindly.

1030.bp: When you see the name 'Washington' in text, does it mean the US state, the capital city, or a person's surname? The answer depends on context and corroborating signals. Multimodal entity linking uses text, images, and structured knowledge together to disambiguate. The challenge is that different modalities offer contradictory clues, and one modality can dominate unfairly, drowning out the others. A fair system balances all signals.
1030.wh: Existing systems either couple all modalities tightly (so one error propagates to all) or use global aggregation (averaging modality signals, which loses nuance). Some entities have clear visual signatures (the Statue of Liberty is distinctive), while others are only identified by text or metadata. Forcing a uniform strategy ignores these differences. The system also needs to know not just if the modalities agree, but precisely how they should agree.
1030.ap: This paper uses expert networks that handle different aspects of the problem in parallel (a divide-and-conquer strategy). Each expert specializes in one type of correspondence—say, visual cues or textual mention patterns. The system learns which experts should matter using a routing mechanism guided by KL divergence (a measure of how different two probability distributions are). It also builds a hierarchical graph showing relationships at multiple levels of detail, and lets the modalities refine each other through this graph rather than just averaging.
1030.ww: By separating the problem into independent experts, one modality's error does not ruin the others. The KL-guided routing means experts learn to specialize: one might focus on visual cues, another on mention patterns, and the system adaptively weights their input. The hierarchical graph captures both coarse (this is a person, not a place) and fine (this is a historical figure, not a celebrity) distinctions.
1030.po: On benchmark datasets for multimodal entity linking, the system consistently ranks higher than prior methods, correctly disambiguating entity mentions even when modalities conflict. The improvements are largest on ambiguous cases where modalities gave contradictory signals.

1031.bp: Complex questions often need multi-step reasoning: 'Which Nobel Prize winners published papers at MIT in the last five years?' requires finding Nobel laureates, checking their MIT affiliations, and verifying recent publications. Typical retrieval-augmented generation systems treat this as one big retrieval problem, but the reasoning and retrieval needed for each step is different. Splitting the task into specialized subtasks could work better.
1031.wh: A single model trying to handle high-level planning (what are the sub-questions?) and detailed execution (find papers on this specific topic) ends up doing both poorly. It gets distracted by irrelevant details while trying to plan, or loses sight of the big picture while executing. Also, different parts of the question benefit from different tools—some need a fact-checking database, others need semantic search.
1031.ap: This paper separates the task into two layers. A high-level planner decomposes the complex question into subtasks and coordinates the overall strategy. For each subtask, a specialized agent equipped with specific tools (knowledge bases, search engines, reasoning modules) handles execution. The planner reasons about how to combine the results from different agents into a final answer. Each agent can focus on its own domain without distraction from the overall goal.
1031.ww: By separating planning from execution, the planner can think strategically without the noise of implementation details. Each specialized agent becomes expert in its domain because it sees only relevant subtasks. This mirrors how humans solve complex problems—we break them down, assign specialists to pieces, then synthesize results—rather than trying to do everything with one person.
1031.po: On complex cross-modal search benchmarks (questions that require combining information from text, tables, and images), this hierarchical approach significantly outperforms flat retrieval-augmented generation systems. The separation of concerns leads to both better reasoning and better execution.

1032.bp: When an AI agent needs to retrieve a table from a database to answer a user's instruction—'find a table with sales data by quarter, excluding 2024'—relevance depends on both topical similarity (sales, quarterly) and following specific constraints (exclude a year, include certain columns). Existing table retrieval systems focus on topical relevance alone and ignore constraints. A system needs to actually follow instructions.
1032.wh: Topical relevance and instruction-following are fundamentally different tasks. A table about 'quarterly sales for all years' is topically relevant but disobeys the 'exclude 2024' instruction. Existing systems have no way to model constraint satisfaction separately from semantic similarity. Also, schema awareness is weak: most systems do not reason carefully about column names and data representation choices.
1032.ap: This paper formalizes a new task: instruction-following table retrieval, where a system must find tables that satisfy both topical relevance and explicit constraints. It introduces a benchmark with tables annotated for inclusion/exclusion requirements and schema constraints. It also proposes a new metric that checks whether retrieval rankings actually adapt to the instruction (compared to ignoring the instruction). The benchmark is large-scale and created via a structured annotation pipeline.
1032.ww: By making constraint satisfaction a formal requirement and measuring it separately, systems can now be trained and evaluated on following instructions. The metric catches systems that do well on topical retrieval but ignore constraints. Schema awareness naturally improves because the benchmark explicitly rewards understanding column semantics and representation choices.
1032.po: The benchmark reveals that existing retrieval models struggle with fine-grained instruction constraints, exhibiting systematic biases toward surface-level semantic cues. By providing the first large-scale evaluation setting for instruction-following table retrieval, it enables future research in this underexplored area and reveals current systems' blind spots.

1033.bp: Generative recommendation systems create a personalized ranking by generating predictions directly, rather than computing similarity scores. Flow matching (a deep generative technique) has been applied here with promise. Yet the standard training objective does not push different users toward different preferences. Without explicit separation between users, the system generates bland, averaged preferences that do not distinguish one person from another.
1033.wh: Directly applying contrastive learning (a technique that pushes different entities apart) to the final output of a flow model causes false repulsion: if two users happen to like the same movie, pushing their scores apart makes the model learn something false. Flow matching is also sensitive to input perturbations, so standard contrastive learning view construction breaks the output—positive pairs become semantically mismatched.
1033.ap: Instead of contrasting the final predictions, this paper applies contrastive learning inside the model, at an intermediate layer (the encoder) before the final output. This avoids the false repulsion problem: even if two users have similar final preferences, their internal representations can still be pushed apart. The system decomposes the flow model into an encoder (shared across users) and a prediction head (per-user), applying contrastive regularization to the encoder representations.
1033.ww: Constraining users' internal representations to be distinct does not force their final preferences to be different. This solves the false repulsion problem: the model learns to represent users differently internally, which naturally leads to personalized outputs without breaking semantic meaning. The encoder-head decomposition provides a clean place to apply the constraint without disrupting the flow-matching process.
1033.po: On collaborative filtering benchmarks, the contrastive flow matching approach generates more diverse and personalized recommendations compared to flow matching with only regression loss. User separation leads to higher-quality rankings where individual preferences come through, not averaged preferences.

1034.bp: LLM-based agents can do complex tasks by calling external tools. But which tool to use? If the tool descriptions are vague ('format: string', 'does conversion'), the agent wastes time trying wrong tools or gives up. This is an acute problem for the Model Context Protocol ecosystem, where thousands of third-party tools exist and descriptions are often unclear. Automating the generation of clear, function-oriented documentation could solve this.
1034.wh: Tool creators write documentation in free-form text, emphasizing human readability over machine searchability. They often hide the actual function signatures inside code, leaving them out of docs entirely. When tools have overlapping names or ambiguous descriptions, an LLM agent retrieving tools sees only noise. The gap between implementation and documentation makes retrieval nearly impossible.
1034.ap: This paper builds an automated pipeline that extracts the actual tool implementation from source code (a white-box analysis), generates precise descriptions for each function based on what the code does, then aggregates these into a structured server-level overview. The pipeline operates in stages: extract tool inventory with metadata, refine each tool's description grounded in its implementation, synthesize a searchable server overview. It also constructs a benchmark of real-world tool discovery queries to measure retrieval quality.
1034.ww: By grounding descriptions in the actual code implementation, there is no gap between documentation and reality. The staged approach (tool-level then server-level) means detailed function information is preserved and then intelligently summarized. The benchmark enables evaluation of retrieval quality, showing whether descriptions are actually useful for finding tools.
1034.po: On a benchmark of 3000+ real open-source MCP servers, the system generates structured documentation that significantly improves tool discovery retrieval compared to raw, unstructured documentation. Agents can now find the right tools more reliably, making complex multi-step tool workflows more practical.
